title: A material with a history
bodyMd:
A fictional design studio tested tiles made with recycled glass. Samples containing a high proportion of recovered material varied more in colour than conventional tiles. A client called the variation a defect. The designers replied that variation could be an intended visual feature, but only if it was disclosed before purchase. They separated that aesthetic question from tests of strength and water absorption, where minimum performance requirements still applied.

The studio’s catalogue therefore showed several tiles from each batch rather than one ideal sample. It also published the relevant test results. The designers did not argue that recycled content excused poor performance. They argued that a product could meet functional requirements while differing from the visual uniformity customers expected. Honest description was needed to make that distinction useful rather than merely promotional.
